findings.title: `cf list tasks` entries missing `completed`/`total` raise `KeyError`, breaking every source
findings.description: `list_tasks` now does `int(e["completed"])` / `int(e["total"])` with no default, so any `cf` version whose `list tasks --json` output omits those keys raises an uncaught `KeyError` — not a `ContextForgeError`. This is a hard boundary: `list_tasks` is called by `_cf_slices_needing_tasks` (sources.py:202) and `_cf_slices_ready_to_implement` (sources.py:254), so both the planning batches and the new `implement-plan` batch fail with a traceback instead of a clean error. The surrounding code in this file consistently uses `e.get("files", [])` / `e.get("designFile")` / `e.get("status", "")` for exactly this reason. The prior `TaskEntry` fields had defaults (`files` defaulted to `[]`), and the new fields should behave the same way (`e.get("completed", 0)`), or the client should raise a `ContextForgeError` naming the field. Note also the design doc (197-slice, "Interfaces Required") lists `completed`/`total` as required cf fields, so the reader cannot assume them — a defensive `.get` is the right call either way.

findings.title: `TaskEntry.completed`/`total` are never populated for the "all tasks checked" readiness check
findings.description: `_not_ready_reason` relies on `task.total > 0 and task.completed == task.total` to flag "all tasks checked but slice not marked complete" (design D2's last row, and success criterion 2). `TaskEntry` now carries those fields and `list_tasks` reads them, but the check is only reachable if cf actually emits them — and the client reads them with `e["completed"]` (see previous finding), so a cf build without those keys crashes the source rather than flagging the item. The two findings compound: the readiness rule that is the stated purpose of the new `completed`/`total` fields has no safe path through the client. The unit test `test_each_not_ready_row` passes `(5, 5)` straight into a stub client, so it never exercises `ContextForgeClient.list_tasks` with a real cf payload — the production shape is untested.

findings.title: A batch that halts leaves the report's `not_run` records un-flagged, so `count()` and `summary_line()` under-report
findings.description: `BatchItemRecord.not_run` sets `outcome=NOT_RUN` but leaves `flag_kind=None`. `BatchReport.count()` counts by outcome only, so `counts` is right, but `render_line()` renders a `not_run` item with no kind — while the Markdown frontmatter carries a `not_run` count. More importantly, `_check_record` in item_resume.py accepts `not_run` records for `--decision retry`, and `_outcome` maps a non-PASSED/ACCEPTED outcome to `ResumeExit.FLAGGED` (exit 1). So a `not_run` item that is retried and succeeds resolves, but a `not_run` item that is retried and halts is recorded as `flagged`/`step_failed` with `decision=retry`, losing the information that it never ran in the original batch. That is arguably intended. The real gap is narrower: `not_run` records are created only for items *after* the in-flight one (`items[position + 1:]`), so the `not_run` set is correct, but the in-flight item is recorded via `from_item(..., flag_kind=FlagKind.STEP_FAILED)` even when the halt was a `GitStateUnknownError` from a *previous* item's branch conflict — the reason text is right but the kind is always `step_failed`, never `branch_conflict`, even when the halt reason is a merge conflict. Success criterion 10 expects a conflicting catch-up to flag the item `branch_conflict`; that path goes through `_flag_kind` (which does classify `BranchFailure.CONFLICT`) for ordinary item failures, but the halt path in `_finish_each_report` hardcodes `STEP_FAILED`. Two sources of truth for the same classification.

findings.title: The `each` step writes the report after every item, doubling the write cost of a large batch
findings.description: `_write_each_report(report, runs_dir, final=False)` runs after *every* item and rewrites both the Markdown and the JSON file through a temp file and a rename. Each write serialises the entire report (all records) twice. For a plan with hundreds of slices this is O(n²) bytes written and O(n) fsync-ish renames, on the hot path of the batch. The design calls for per-item writes (D7), so the behaviour is intended, but the report grows linearly while the writes grow quadratically — a mitigation would be to write the JSON incrementally or to write per-item but only re-serialise the changed portion. Worth noting the write is already correctly off the event loop (`asyncio.to_thread`), so this is a throughput concern rather than a loop-blocking bug.

findings.title: `_locked` closes the coroutine but the resume path never takes the lock through it
findings.description: `_locked` wraps `asyncio.run` and takes the project lock around it for mutating pipelines — good. But the item-resume path (`handle_item_resume` → `resume_item`) takes the lock itself inside `item_resume.resume_item`, on a *different* lock acquisition from the same `run_lock.project_run_lock`. Two acquisition sites for the same lock is a duplication risk: the exit codes differ (`run.py` exits 2 on lock failure, `item_resume` returns `ResumeExit.REJECTED`, also 2), but the error handling differs — `run.py` prints a red message and exits 2, `item_resume` returns an outcome that `run_item._print` renders. The lock's own docstring and `run_lock.py` are clean, but the "who takes the lock" decision is now spread across two modules. This is consistent with the design (D11 says the lock is taken by item resume *and* by `sq run`), so it is not a defect — but a single `take_lock_or_exit` helper shared by both would remove the risk of the two paths drifting.

findings.title: `run_item.handle_item_resume` imports private functions from `run.py`, creating a circular import
findings.description: `run_item.py` imports `_apply_param_overrides` and `_run_pipeline_sdk` from `run.py` inside the function body, and `run.py` imports `check_item_flags` and `handle_item_resume` from `run_item.py` at module level. The deferred import avoids an import-time cycle, but it means the two CLI command modules are mutually dependent and the `pyright: ignore[reportPrivateUsage]` comments are papering over the resulting type errors. The cleaner arrangement is to move `_apply_param_overrides` and `_run_pipeline_sdk` into a shared module (e.g. `run_common.py`) that both import, or to pass them into `handle_item_resume` as parameters from `run.py`, which already holds them.

findings.title: `_apply_param_overrides` raises `typer.BadParameter` inside the item-resume path, where the exit code contract is 2 (REJECTED) not 1
findings.description: `check_item_flags` raises `typer.Exit(USAGE_EXIT)` where `USAGE_EXIT = int(ResumeExit.REJECTED)` = 2, matching the D8 table. But a reserved `-p` key on an item resume goes through `_apply_param_overrides`, which raises `typer.BadParameter` — Typer renders that as a usage error with exit code 2 as well, so the code coincidentally matches. However the *message* differs from the reserved-key message the other paths produce, and the test `test_a_reserved_p_key_on_an_item_resume_exits_2` only asserts the exit code, not the message. The D8 contract says a refusal names the fact that refused it; the reserved-key refusal currently produces Typer's generic "Invalid value for '--param'" rendering rather than `'accept_decision' is reserved; use --decision accept`. The dedicated `item_params` check in `item_resume.py:283-285` produces the right message, but it is unreachable for `-p` keys because `_apply_param_overrides` rejects them first. The two reserved-key guards should produce one message.

findings.title: `_outcome` uses `next(...)` without a default, so a missing record raises `StopIteration` inside a coroutine
findings.description: `_outcome` does `record = next(r for r in run.report.records if r.index == index)`. `StopIteration` raised inside an `async def` is converted by the runtime into a `RuntimeError: coroutine raised StopIteration`, which is not caught by `resume_item`'s handlers (`_Stop`, `GitEnvironmentError`, `OSError`) and escapes to the CLI as an unhandled traceback rather than a clean exit code. The path is reachable only if the report is mutated between validation and outcome (e.g. the body replaced a record whose `index` differs from `request.index`), but the function has no guard and the failure mode is opaque. A `next(..., None)` plus an explicit `_Stop(REJECTED, ...)` would be the fail-fast behaviour the guidelines require.

findings.title: `_write_atomic` leaves the temp file behind when the rename fails
findings.description: `tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(..., delete=False)` creates the temp file; if `temp.replace(target)` raises `OSError`, the `except OSError` block logs and re-raises, but the temp file is never removed. Every failed report write therefore leaves a `.{name}.{random}` file in the runs directory. The runs directory is also globbed by `StateManager.list_runs` for `*.json` — the temp file is named `.{target.name}.XXXX` where target is e.g. `run.slices.report.json`, so the temp file is `.run.slices.report.json.abc123` and does *not* end in `.json`, so `list_runs` will not pick it up. But `BatchReport.load` globs nothing, so the residue is inert clutter rather than a correctness bug — still, it accumulates in the user's config directory on every failed write. A `finally` that unlinks the temp file when the replace failed would be correct.

findings.title: Reserved control params are centralised and enforced at every entry point
findings.description: `OVERRIDE_INSTRUCTIONS` and `ACCEPT_DECISION` are defined once and imported by `executor.py`, `actions/dispatch.py`, `loader.py` and `run.py` — no scattered string literals remain (verified by grep: the only other occurrences are the `CheckpointDecision.override_instructions` field name and the `_prompt_checkpoint_interactive` local, which are unrelated). The loader rejects both in a pipeline's `params:` block, `run.py` rejects them as `-p` keys, and `item_params` strips them from loaded run state with a WARNING.

findings.title: The run lock is correctly POSIX-guarded, non-blocking, and released on process death
findings.description: `fcntl` is imported inside the function so the module imports on Windows, the lock is `LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB` so a busy lock fails at once rather than waiting, and the descriptor is closed in a `finally` so the `flock` drops — including when the holder is SIGKILLed, which the test `test_a_killed_holder_releases_the_lock` verifies with a real subprocess. The lock lives in `{git dir}`, which is per worktree, so separate worktrees still run in parallel (also tested).

findings.title: The dependency ordering is a correct stable topological sort with a named cycle
findings.description: `order_by_dependencies` uses a min-heap over input positions, so ties break by plan order, and only dependencies between returned items count. The cycle path is reconstructed by `_find_cycle` and names the cycle (`196 → 197 → 196`), which the tests assert for both two- and three-node cycles.

findings.title: The report's JSON form round-trips and refuses a mismatched schema version
findings.description: `BatchReport.load` checks `schemaVersion` before reading anything and names both versions on a mismatch; `to_json`/`from_json` round-trip the records exactly (asserted by `test_round_trip`). `StateManager.list_runs` skips `*.report.json` so a batch report beside a run state is not read as a broken run.
